0.title: The Letter of Jude: Contend for the Faith
0.overview:
Jude is one of the most neglected letters in the New Testament. Most Christians know the doxology at the end — and it is magnificent — but could not tell you what comes before it. What comes before it is some of the most urgent, vivid and pastoral writing in the whole Bible. Jude is a fire-bell.

The author identifies himself as “a servant of Jesus Christ and brother of James” (v. 1). He does not say “brother of the Lord” — though he almost certainly was. Matthew 13:55 and Mark 6:3 name “Judas” among the brothers of Jesus, and James was the recognised head of the Jerusalem church. Jude had credentials that would have opened every door in the early Christian world: raised in the same household as the Son of God, converted after the resurrection, brother to the most respected Jewish-Christian leader of the first generation. He uses none of it. He calls himself a servant of Jesus Christ. The family tie, once the most important fact about him, has given way to a greater one: since the resurrection, Jesus is first of all his Lord. He no longer has a brother who happens to be the Messiah; he has a Lord who happens to have been his brother.

The occasion for the letter is stated plainly in v. 3. Jude had intended to write about “our common salvation” — a warm, constructive letter celebrating the faith they shared. He never wrote it. The crisis was too pressing. False teachers had “crept in unnoticed” (v. 4), and Jude found himself writing an alarm instead of a celebration. The letter we have is not the letter he planned. This matters pastorally: faithful ministry sometimes means setting aside what we intended to say in order to say what the moment requires.

How is Jude related to 2 Peter 2, which says many of the same things? Most scholars think Peter knew Jude’s letter and adapted it, and that is the more likely reading; some think Jude used 2 Peter, or that both drew on common teaching. That takes nothing from either: an inspired writer may use another’s words, as the prophets and apostles often did.

The letter is twenty-five verses. It has no chapter breaks. It is a single sustained argument that moves from the alarm (vv. 3–4), through the evidence (vv. 5–16), to the counter-strategy for the faithful (vv. 17–23), and finally to one of the greatest doxologies in Scripture (vv. 24–25). The fire and the doxology belong together. The letter that begins with danger ends with adoration, and the adoration is not a way of escaping the danger. It is the ground on which the whole letter stands. You can contend for the faith without bitterness, rescue others without losing yourself and hold on under pressure, because the One who keeps you is infinitely more powerful than everything that threatens you.

1.title: Contend, Hold Fast, Adore
1.overview:
Jude’s one chapter moves in four steps. He states why he writes: contend for the faith, because false teachers have slipped in (vv. 3–4). He gives the evidence: three examples of judgment on people who had privilege and despised it (vv. 5–7), then a vivid portrait of the false teachers who are repeating the pattern (vv. 8–16). He turns to the faithful: remember, build up, pray, keep yourselves in God’s love and rescue the wavering (vv. 17–23). And he ends with God, who is able to keep his people from stumbling (vv. 24–25).

The order matters. The darkness of vv. 5–16 is framed by a people who are kept (v. 1) and the God who is able to keep them (v. 24). Jude warns in order to make his readers brave, not anxious: the courage of people who know they are held.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Before any warning, Jude tells the church who they are: called (God summoned them), beloved in God the Father (they rest in his love now) and kept for Jesus Christ (guarded until he comes). Every alarm that follows is heard by people God is holding.
verseByVerse.theology:
Called, Beloved, Kept

The security of believers rests on God’s call, love and keeping, not on their own grip.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: A church shaken by false teachers is first reminded of its security.

Now: A believer who fears drifting away begins where Jude begins: not with their grip on God, but with his grip on them.

verseByVerse.quote: Jude, a servant of Jesus Christ and brother of James, To those who are called, beloved in God the Father and kept for Jesus Christ: May mercy, peace, and love be multiplied to you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. Jude is a short, urgent letter calling believers to contend for the faith against ungodly intruders who turn God’s grace into sensuality and deny Jesus Christ (vv. 3–4). He recalls God’s judgments on unbelieving Israel, the fallen angels and Sodom (vv. 5–7), portrays the intruders through Cain, Balaam and Korah and five pictures from nature (vv. 8–13), and cites Enoch and the apostles (vv. 14–19). Then he tells believers how to stand and how to rescue the wavering (vv. 20–23). The whole alarm is framed by two words about God: at the start his people are kept; at the end he is able to keep them.

The setting. Jude (Judas) was a brother of James and of Jesus (Mark 6:3). He did not believe in Jesus during his ministry (John 7:5) but came to faith after the resurrection (Acts 1:14). The date is uncertain, perhaps AD 60–80, and the readers unknown, probably Jewish Christians. Much of the letter parallels 2 Peter 2. This man grew up in the same house as Jesus, in a family that once thought Jesus out of his mind (Mark 3:21). Now he writes of Jesus Christ as our only Master and Lord.

Jude, a servant of Jesus Christ. “Servant” (doulos) is slave: one whose will belongs to another. Jude was a brother of Jesus, which only James among the other New Testament writers could also say, and like James (James 1:1) he chose not to mention it. This is not false modesty. Before Easter, Jude had a brother; after Easter, he had a Lord. When Jude calls himself a slave of Jesus, he is confessing that Jesus rose and that this changed everything. The relationship that matters is not physical family but faith (Mark 3:35).

And brother of James. James was the well-known leader of the Jerusalem church (Galatians 2:9). Jude names him not to claim status but to establish identity.

To those who are called. Three descriptions of the readers follow. “Called” (klētois) is the call of God that actually brings a person to faith (Romans 8:28–30), often named his effectual call. It is God’s act, not their initiative.

Beloved in God the Father. “Beloved” (ēgapēmenois) is in a Greek tense that means loved and still loved. They live inside the Father’s unchanging love. Before Jude says a word about danger, he tells them where they live.

And kept for Jesus Christ. “Kept” (tetērēmenois) is the same tense: guarded and still guarded, as a treasure is kept for its owner, or a bride for her bridegroom. Their safety does not rest on their own hold; God is holding them.

The Father’s gift to the Son. Why would the Father keep a people for Jesus Christ? Because they are his gift to his Son, and it is the Father’s will that he should lose nothing of all that he has been given (John 6:37–39). The whole letter of warning is written to people the Father has promised his Son he will not lose.

If I am kept, why does this letter warn me so strongly? Because warnings are one of the ways God keeps his people. A father who holds his child’s hand on a cliff path also says, “Stay away from the edge.” The warning does not mean he might let go; it is part of how he holds. Jude will tell you to keep yourselves in the love of God (v. 21), and then end by praising the God who keeps you (v. 24). Read every warning in this letter as the voice of the One who is guarding you, not as a sign that he might fail.

Mercy, peace, and love. “Multiplied” (plēthyntheiē) is increased, abundant. In a letter about danger, Jude opens with what God gives: mercy that does not hold failures against them, peace that holds the heart steady, and love that holds them no matter what. Those who must contend need more of all three, not less.

In everyday life. Before you face anything hard today, a difficult conversation, a temptation, a worrying piece of news, say these three words to yourself: called, loved, kept. They are true of every believer: God did this for you, and it still holds today.
verseByVerse.note: Jude (Judas) was a brother of James and of Jesus, who, like James, came to faith after the resurrection. Much of his letter is closely paralleled in 2 Peter 2.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jude meant to write a warm letter about “our common salvation”, but the danger forced him to write an alarm instead. The result is a key sentence about the church and its teaching: the faith has been given, it is complete, and it must be guarded.
verseByVerse.theology:
Contend for the Faith

The faith was delivered once for all to the saints. False teachers turn grace into sensuality and deny the only Master and Lord, Jesus Christ.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Jude set aside the letter he wanted to write because the danger was urgent.

Now: Contend as someone who loves the people being misled, not as someone who enjoys a fight.

verseByVerse.quote: Beloved, although I was very eager to write to you about our common salvation, I found it necessary to write appealing to you to contend for the faith that was once for all delivered to the saints. For certain people have crept in unnoticed who long ago were designated for this condemnation, ungodly people, who pervert the grace of our God into sensuality and deny our only Master and Lord, Jesus Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Our common salvation. “Common salvation” (koinēs sōtērias) is the salvation all believers share, Jew and Gentile, slave and free. Jude had planned a celebratory letter about it, and it was never written. He is not a man who enjoys a fight; he is a pastor who would have preferred to celebrate. It is the people who love the gospel most who find it hardest to watch it being distorted.

Contend for the faith. “Contend” (epagōnizesthai) is to fight earnestly, as an athlete strains in a contest; it is related to our word agony. “The faith” (tē pistei) is not personal trust here, but the body of truth believed, the gospel.

Once for all delivered. “Once for all” (hapax) is a single, final, complete delivery. “Delivered” (paradotheisē) is handed down, entrusted like a precious deposit. The faith was given by God through the apostles, complete; nothing can be added to it or subtracted from it. This is why no book can be added to the Bible and why Scripture alone is the final authority. And it was delivered to the saints, not to an elite: every believer is entrusted with it.

What is the faith that was once for all delivered? The body of apostolic teaching about Christ, given complete and not to be added to: who he is, God and man; what he did, in his life, death for sinners, resurrection and ascension; what he will do, in his return and judgment; and how sinners are saved, by grace through faith, and called to holy lives. That is why the church has no new revelation to wait for; it has a faith to keep. And contending for it means teaching it clearly, holding it fast, exposing error and rescuing those caught by it (vv. 22–23), with the gentleness of a servant of the Lord (2 Timothy 2:24–25), not the bitterness of a quarreller.

Crept in unnoticed. “Crept in unnoticed” (pareisedysan) is slipped in sideways, like spies entering by a side door. They came the way dangerous teaching almost always comes: gradually, plausibly, using the church’s own language. The most dangerous false teaching sounds like the gospel while quietly removing its foundations.

Designated for this condemnation. “Designated” (progegrammenoi) is written beforehand, marked out in advance. Their judgment is no surprise to God: Scripture announced the judgment of people who pervert his grace long before these men appeared.

Does “long ago were designated for this condemnation” mean that God predestined these people to be condemned? Some read it as God’s decree; others as the condemnation long foretold in Scripture for people like them, which Jude goes on to show with Israel, the angels, Sodom and Enoch’s prophecy. The word itself most naturally means written beforehand, and Jude’s following examples suggest that the condemnation of such people was written in Scripture long ago. Behind that writing stands God’s sovereign governance of all things, so that nothing about these men takes him by surprise. But their sin is their own: they perverted grace into sensuality, and they are justly judged for what they freely chose.

Ungodly people. “Ungodly” (asebeis) is irreverent, without regard for God. It is a key word of Jude (vv. 4, 15, 18). They may be religious, but God is not feared in their lives.

Pervert the grace of our God. “Pervert” (metatithentes) is to change, turn into something else. “Sensuality” (aselgeia) is unrestrained immorality. They twisted grace into a licence to sin, reasoning that since we are forgiven, sin does not matter (Romans 6:1–2). Any teaching that produces loose living rather than holiness has not understood grace; it has put something else in its place. The grace of our God does not permit sin; it frees us from sin’s power and teaches us to walk in holiness.

Our only Master and Lord. “Master” (despotēs) is a sovereign owner, and “Lord” (kyrios) is the one who rules. In the Greek both titles belong to Jesus Christ, a strong statement of his deity: Master is the title the first believers gave to God himself in prayer (Luke 2:29; Acts 4:24). The intruders denied his lordship by their lives and perhaps by their teaching (Titus 1:16). To twist grace into permission to sin is already to deny him as Lord.

Where Christians differ: is the faith still developing through new revelation? Some churches hold that doctrine develops through ongoing revelation or the church’s teaching office, adding new dogmas over time; some charismatics expect new prophetic revelation. Many charismatic believers who expect prophecy today agree that it may never add to Scripture or overrule it, and they love the Bible as warmly as anyone. This commentary’s view: Jude says the faith was delivered once for all. The apostolic deposit is complete. The church’s understanding of Scripture may deepen, but no new doctrine may be added. Scripture alone is the final rule of faith, and the canon is closed.

Does stressing grace not lead people to take sin lightly? Real grace never does. The grace that forgives also transforms: it unites us to Christ, gives us a new heart, and teaches us to say no to ungodliness (Titus 2:11–12). Those who use grace as an excuse show that they have not received it. The answer to the idea that Christians may ignore God’s law (antinomianism) is not less grace, as if the gospel needed to be balanced with a little law to keep people in line, but a true understanding of grace. People who have truly been forgiven much love much, and love keeps God’s commandments (John 14:15).

How do I contend without becoming a contentious person? Contend for the faith, not for your preferences, and contend about what matters most: the person and work of Christ, the gospel of grace, the holiness it produces. Know your Bible well enough to do it. Speak the truth in love (Ephesians 4:15), gently, without mockery, seeking to win people rather than to defeat them. Distinguish between those who teach error and those who have been confused by it (vv. 22–23). And pray for those you disagree with. A contender who does not pray for his opponents has become a quarreller.

In everyday life. Take one central truth this week, for example the deity of Christ, justification by faith or the return of Christ, and learn to explain it simply with two or three Bible passages.

For worship. The faith was delivered once for all, because the Saviour did his work once for all: he lived the perfect life, died the one death that atones, rose and reigns, and nothing needs to be added. Over this grace stands our only Master and Lord, who bought his people and will not let them be stolen.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Three examples make one point: privilege does not protect from judgment. Israel was redeemed from Egypt; the angels stood in God’s presence; Sodom had righteous Lot in its midst. Each had unusual exposure to God, turned from him, and was judged.
verseByVerse.theology:
Privilege Is No Shield

Outward privilege is no substitute for persevering faith.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The false teachers belonged to the church but were walking the same road as unbelieving Israel, the fallen angels and Sodom.

Now: The person most at risk is not the one who has never heard, but the one who has heard so often that the gospel has become background noise.

verseByVerse.quote: Now I want to remind you, although you once fully knew it, that Jesus, who saved a people out of the land of Egypt, afterward destroyed those who did not believe. And the angels who did not stay within their own position of authority, but left their proper dwelling, he has kept in eternal chains under gloomy darkness until the judgment of the great day — just as Sodom and Gomorrah and the surrounding cities, which likewise indulged in sexual immorality and pursued unnatural desire, serve as an example by undergoing a punishment of eternal fire.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I want to remind you. They knew these truths; they needed reminding (2 Peter 1:12). Jude, like Peter, believes that the church’s great need is not novelty but memory.

Jesus, who saved a people. The manuscripts differ: some have the Lord, others Jesus, others God. Jesus has strong early support and is probably original, since copyists were more likely to change it to the Lord than to bring Jesus into an Old Testament scene. If so, Jude says that Christ, before he became man, brought Israel out of Egypt, as Paul also says (1 Corinthians 10:4, 9). The same Jesus who would later become flesh opened the sea, fed them with bread from heaven, and gave them water from the rock that was himself. In either reading, salvation and judgment belong to the same Lord.

Afterward destroyed. “Afterward” (to deuteron) is literally the second time: first he saved, then he judged. Israel refused to trust the God who had brought them out of Egypt, and the generation aged twenty and over, except Caleb and Joshua, died in the wilderness (Numbers 14:29–30; Hebrews 3:16–19). No privilege, whether the exodus then or baptism and church membership now, can take the place of persevering faith.

Does this mean that the saved can perish? Israel as a nation was brought out of Egypt, but the generation who did not believe died in the wilderness. Outward deliverance and membership among God’s people are not the same as saving faith. Some read the example as a warning that true believers may be lost; the more likely reading is that it warns professing believers not to trust in privileges without faith. Jude himself has just called believers kept for Jesus Christ (v. 1), and he will end by praising the God who is able to keep them from stumbling (v. 24).

The angels. The second example. “Position of authority” (archē) is rule, domain, rank. These beings stood before the throne of God, and they left their assigned place. Jewish tradition, especially 1 Enoch (a Jewish writing from the centuries before Christ, outside the Bible), connected this with the sons of God and the daughters of men (Genesis 6:1–4). Peter refers to the same angels (2 Peter 2:4).

Their proper dwelling. “Proper dwelling” (oikētērion) is home, habitation: heaven. They walked out of the presence of God.

Kept in eternal chains. A wordplay: they did not keep (tērēsantas) their position, so God keeps (tetērēken) them in chains. Believers are kept for Jesus Christ (v. 1); these angels are kept for judgment. High rank does not shield anyone from judgment; it makes them more answerable.

Who are these angels? Some take them as the angels who fell with Satan at the beginning; many Jewish and early Christian readers, and many today, link them with the sons of God of Genesis 6:2, pointing to Jude’s next words, that Sodom “likewise” sinned sexually. Calvin and many Reformed writers read the sons of God in Genesis 6 as the godly line of Seth instead, and some take them as kings. This commentary leaves the question open, as Genesis 6 does, and the point stands either way: God judges rebellion and rescues his own.

If these angels are in chains, why are demons still active? Jude speaks of a particular group confined until the judgment, not of all fallen angels; others are still at work under God’s restraint (Ephesians 6:12; 1 Peter 5:8).

Sodom and Gomorrah. The third example. The surrounding cities were Admah and Zeboiim (Deuteronomy 29:23), the cities of the plain.

Unnatural desire. “Likewise”: like the angels, they crossed boundaries God set. “Unnatural desire” (sarkos heteras) is literally other flesh. The phrase may cover both pursuing flesh of a different kind (the visitors were angels, though the men did not know it) and desire contrary to God’s design.

What was the sin of Sodom? Ezekiel names pride, excess and neglect of the poor (Ezekiel 16:49), and Genesis shows the men of the city demanding sex with Lot’s visitors (Genesis 19:5). Jude adds that they indulged in sexual immorality and pursued unnatural desire. The visitors were angels, but the men of Sodom took them for men; their desire was against the created order, and Jude names it as sexual sin. The passage agrees with the rest of Scripture that same-sex sexual practice is sin, among the other sins of a proud and godless city. The clearest passages are Leviticus 18:22, Romans 1:26–27 and 1 Corinthians 6:9–11, read in the light of God’s pattern for marriage as one man and one woman (Genesis 2:24), which Jesus himself reaffirmed (Matthew 19:4–6).

An example. “Example” (deigma) is a sample, a display. The cities of the plain became a permanent warning sign, and the fire that fell on them a sample of the eternal fire of the final judgment (Matthew 25:41), which is still coming. And yet the same Jesus came down to bear judgment for those who believe, so that the fire they deserved fell on him instead.

Where Christians differ: is punishment eternal, or do the wicked cease to exist? Annihilationists hold that the wicked are destroyed and cease to exist; universalists that all are eventually saved. Some evangelical believers hold the first view, pointing to Scripture’s language of destruction, and they do so out of reverence for the Bible, not to escape it. This commentary’s view: Jude speaks of eternal chains and eternal fire (vv. 6–7) and utter darkness reserved forever (v. 13). Jesus used the same word, eternal, for both punishment and life (Matthew 25:46). Scripture teaches conscious, eternal punishment for those who reject God (Revelation 14:11; 20:10). This truth is held with sorrow and with urgency to warn and to rescue (v. 23).

How can a loving God punish for ever? Because sin is not a small offence against a small god, but rebellion against the infinitely holy and good Creator, and because those who persist in rejecting him go on rejecting him. Hell is God giving people, justly, what they chose: life without him, which is darkness. We must not soften what Jesus himself taught more than anyone. But the same God who will judge has done the most costly thing imaginable to rescue us: he sent his Son to bear the fire in our place. The doctrine of hell is not a reason to doubt his love but a measure of it, and a summons to run to Christ and to warn others.

I experience same-sex attraction, or love someone who does. What does this mean for us? It means you are not a special category of sinner; every believer battles disordered desires, and temptation itself is not sin. The call is the same for all Christians: to deny ourselves, take up the cross, and follow Christ in holiness, which for every unmarried believer means chastity. The church must be a place where such believers are welcomed, loved, befriended and supported, not shamed or isolated. And for anyone who has fallen, the word of 1 Corinthians 6:11 stands: such were some of you, but you were washed. Christ receives all who come.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–13 — The False Teachers: A Portrait
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jude paints the false teachers in image after image, from Cain, Balaam and Korah to reefs, rainless clouds and wandering stars. Each image describes people who promise nourishment and give nothing, or worse.
verseByVerse.theology:
A Portrait of False Teachers

Where even the archangel left judgment to the Lord, these men speak with contempt about what they do not understand.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: They shared the church’s love feasts while feeding only themselves.

Now: Beware teaching that looks impressive and spiritual but leaves people no closer to Christ and no more holy.

verseByVerse.quote: Yet in like manner these people also, relying on their dreams, defile the flesh, reject authority, and blaspheme the glorious ones. But when the archangel Michael, contending with the devil, was disputing about the body of Moses, he did not presume to pronounce a blasphemous judgment, but said, “The Lord rebuke you.” But these people blaspheme all that they do not understand, and they are destroyed by all that they, like unreasoning animals, understand instinctively. Woe to them! For they walked in the way of Cain and abandoned themselves for the sake of gain to Balaam’s error and perished in Korah’s rebellion. These are hidden reefs at your love feasts, as they feast with you without fear, shepherds feeding themselves; waterless clouds, swept along by winds; fruitless trees in late autumn, twice dead, uprooted; wild waves of the sea, casting up the foam of their own shame; wandering stars, for whom the gloom of utter darkness has been reserved forever.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Relying on their dreams. “Relying on their dreams” (enypniazomenoi) is claiming visions and revelations as authority for their teaching and conduct. It is an old problem. False prophets said, “I have dreamed”, and God answered that they prophesied the deceit of their own heart (Jeremiah 23:25–32). The claim is still heard: “God told me directly”, offered as a reason to set aside what God has revealed publicly and permanently.

Three charges. They defile the flesh, as Sodom did; they reject authority, as unbelieving Israel and the angels did; and they blaspheme the glorious ones. “Glorious ones” (doxas) are angelic beings, as in 2 Peter 2:10, of whom they speak with contempt. The false teachers are repeating the old sins all at once.

The body of Moses. The dispute over Moses’ body comes not from the Old Testament but from a Jewish tradition, perhaps recorded in a lost work called the Assumption of Moses. God buried Moses (Deuteronomy 34:5–6), and the tradition said the devil claimed his body. Michael is the archangel who protects God’s people (Daniel 12:1; Revelation 12:7).

He did not presume. Michael, mighty as he was, left judgment to God (compare Zechariah 3:2, where the angel of the LORD says the same to Satan). He, with far more authority than the false teachers, showed far more restraint.

The Lord who rebukes the devil. The archangel would not pronounce judgment, but he knew who would: the Lord. In the Gospels that Lord stands on earth, saying, “Be gone, Satan!” (Matthew 4:10), and rebuking unclean spirits with a word (Mark 1:25). In Revelation the accuser is thrown down and the saints conquer him by the blood of the Lamb (Revelation 12:7–11). The authority to judge the devil, which the false teachers grabbed and the archangel declined, belongs to Christ, and at the cross he used it to defeat him.

Should Christians rebuke the devil, then? Even the archangel did not pronounce judgment on him in his own authority, but left it to God: “The Lord rebuke you.” Believers are to resist the devil by faith, God’s word and prayer (James 4:7; 1 Peter 5:8–9; Ephesians 6:11–18), not to mock him, address him with bravado or claim authority to bind him. The battle is the Lord’s.

All that they do not understand. Arrogance born of ignorance. The less they know, the more freely they speak.

Like unreasoning animals. What they do understand, their instincts and appetites, is what destroys them (2 Peter 2:12). They claim a higher knowledge of spiritual things, but the only knowledge they really have is what an animal has: appetite.

The way of Cain. One woe and three examples: Cain, Balaam and Korah. “Woe” is a prophet’s announcement of judgment, as in Jesus’ woes on the Pharisees (Matthew 23). Cain came to God in his own way and killed the brother whose offering God accepted (Genesis 4; 1 John 3:12): religion on one’s own terms, turning into hatred of the righteous.

Balaam’s error. Balaam represents greed: a man to whom God had truly spoken, who put himself up for hire and led God’s people into immorality and idolatry for a fee (Numbers 22–25; 31:16; 2 Peter 2:15). “Abandoned themselves” is literally poured themselves out, rushed headlong: not a slip but a plunge.

Korah’s rebellion. Korah represents rebellion against God’s appointed leaders, for which the earth swallowed him (Numbers 16). “Perished” is past tense: their end is so certain that Jude speaks of it as done. Hatred, greed and proud rebellion: the false teachers walk in all three.

Hidden reefs. Five pictures from nature follow. “Hidden reefs” (spilades) are rocks below the water, on which ships are wrecked; the word can also mean stains. “Love feasts” (agapais) were the church’s fellowship meals, often with the Lord’s Supper. A reef looks like calm water until the hull tears open.

Shepherds feeding themselves. “Without fear” (aphobōs) is without reverence, at the very table where Christ’s death was remembered. Shepherds feeding themselves is the exact opposite of a pastor’s calling (Ezekiel 34:2, 8): shepherds exist to feed the flock, not to feed from it.

Waterless clouds. Clouds that promise rain but give none (Proverbs 25:14, where a man who boasts of a gift he does not give is like clouds and wind without rain). In a dry land, clouds on the horizon meant hope; waterless clouds raise hope and give nothing.

Fruitless trees. Trees that should bear fruit at harvest but have none (Matthew 7:17–19). “Twice dead”: dead in fruitlessness and dead with roots torn up; perhaps spiritually dead and destined for the second death (Revelation 20:14). As Jesus said, “Every plant that my heavenly Father has not planted will be rooted up” (Matthew 15:13).

Wild waves. Restless, raging, leaving filthy foam and debris on the beach (Isaiah 57:20, where the wicked are like the tossing sea, whose waters toss up mire and dirt). All noise and energy, and only rubbish left behind.

Wandering stars. “Wandering stars” (asteres planētai) are planets or shooting stars, or perhaps fallen angels in Jewish imagery. Sailors navigated by the fixed stars; a star that wanders leads them astray, as the teacher who will not hold the apostolic faith misleads those trying to find the way. Those who would not shine with a steady light will lose all light.

Five pictures, one diagnosis. The five images are taken from sea, sky and land, and each is a broken promise: a reef that looks like calm water, a cloud that looks like rain, a tree that looks like harvest, a wave that looks like power, a star that looks like a guide. Each delivers nothing, or worse. That is what false teaching is.

Textual note. Jude draws on Jewish traditions that are not in the Old Testament, here and in verses 14–15. Quoting or alluding to a writing does not make that writing Scripture; Paul quoted pagan poets (Acts 17:28; Titus 1:12). Because Jude wrote by the Spirit, the particular point he cites is true.

Someone tells me God gave them a dream or a word for me. How should I respond? Kindly, but with Scripture in hand. This commentary holds that new revelatory gifts ceased with the apostles, though we hold that view charitably toward brothers who differ. The reason is that Scripture calls the apostles and prophets the church’s foundation (Ephesians 2:20), laid once, and Jude says the faith was delivered once for all (v. 3); many charismatic believers, for their part, agree that any word today must be tested by Scripture and can never add to it. Either way, no dream or word may contradict Scripture, add to the faith once delivered, or override plain obedience. If what is said agrees with the Bible, you need the Bible, not the dream, to know it is true. If it disagrees, set it aside, however sincere the person. And be especially wary of any claimed revelation that excuses sin, demands money, or puts a leader beyond question; that is exactly what Jude describes.

How can I tell whether a church leader is feeding the flock or himself? Watch what he does with Scripture, people, money and correction. A true shepherd opens the word faithfully and points to Christ, not himself. He knows and cares for ordinary members, especially the weak and the troubled. He is open about money and does not live off the flock lavishly. He welcomes accountability and can be corrected. A self-feeding shepherd is the reverse: his sermons centre on himself, he courts the influential, he is evasive about finances, and he punishes those who question him. Where a leader abuses people, it must be brought into the light and the victims protected; Christ’s sheep are not his to use.

In everyday life. In the places where you lead, at home, at work, in a small group, are you feeding others or feeding yourself? Is there any of Cain’s envy, Balaam’s love of gain, or Korah’s resentment of authority in you? Name it before God today; he exposes it in order to forgive it (1 John 1:9).

For worship. Against every image of failure stands Christ: the rock on which no one is wrecked, the living water that never runs dry, the true vine, the Lord who stills the waves, the bright morning star. Cain killed his brother; Christ died for his brothers. Balaam sold his gift; Christ gave himself freely. Korah grasped at authority; Christ, who had all authority, took the form of a servant. He is the Good Shepherd who feeds the sheep and lays down his life for them.
verseByVerse.note: The dispute over Moses’ body is not in the Old Testament; it was known from Jewish tradition. Cain, Balaam and Korah stand for murderous hatred, greed and rebellion.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jude quotes a prophecy found in 1 Enoch, a Jewish book widely read in his day, without saying the book is Scripture. Its message matches the rest of the Bible (Daniel 7:10; Matthew 25:31).
verseByVerse.theology:
The Prophecy of Enoch

The Lord will come with his holy ones to judge the ungodly for their deeds and their words.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The false teachers grumbled, boasted and flattered people for gain.

Now: A true shepherd says what people need to hear; a false one says what pays.

verseByVerse.quote: It was also about these that Enoch, the seventh from Adam, prophesied, saying, 'Behold, the Lord comes with ten thousands of his holy ones, to execute judgment on all and to convict all the ungodly of all their deeds of ungodliness that they have committed in such an ungodly way, and of all the harsh things that ungodly sinners have spoken against him.' These are grumblers, malcontents, following their own sinful desires; they are loud-mouthed boasters, showing favoritism to gain advantage.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Enoch, the seventh from Adam. Enoch walked with God and was taken (Genesis 5:18–24; Hebrews 11:5); with Elijah, he is one of two people in Scripture of whom it is said that they did not die. “Seventh from Adam” counts Adam as the first, a description found in 1 Enoch itself. So before the flood, this man was already warning of the Lord’s coming. Jude quotes 1 Enoch 1:9, a prophecy perhaps preserved by tradition from Enoch himself.

Ten thousands of his holy ones. “Comes” (ēlthen) is literally came: the future spoken of as past, because it is as certain as if already done. “Ten thousands” (myriasin) is myriads, an uncountable multitude. “Holy ones” are angels (Deuteronomy 33:2; Matthew 25:31). The sheer number tells of a judgment no one can resist.

The coming Lord has a name. In 1 Enoch the one who comes is God. Jude, who has just called Jesus our only Master and Lord (v. 4), most likely understands the coming Lord to be the risen Jesus: the Son of Man will come in his glory, and all the angels with him (Matthew 25:31), for the Father has given all judgment to the Son (John 5:22). The brother Jude once did not believe is the Judge before whom every harsh word will be answered for. And yet this same Lord, before he comes in glory, came in humility: the Judge stood in the dock, was convicted in our place, and bore the sentence. So the day that will expose the ungodly holds no terror for those who are hidden in him.

To convict all the ungodly. “Convict” (elenxai) is a legal word: to prove guilty conclusively before a court. The ungodly will be proved guilty, so plainly that even they cannot deny it. “Ungodly” appears four times in one sentence: their whole character is ungodliness.

Harsh things. “Harsh things” (sklērōn) are hard, defiant words. God judges words as well as deeds (Matthew 12:36–37). Every careless sneer at God, every mocking word against his Christ, is heard and recorded.

Grumblers, malcontents. “Grumblers” (gongystai) are murmurers, like Israel in the wilderness (1 Corinthians 10:10); the word sounds like a low discontented muttering. “Malcontents” (mempsimoiroi) are complainers about their lot, who always find something wrong with what God has given them.

Their own sinful desires. Their complaints and their lusts are connected: a heart that will not be content with God’s provision goes looking for its own.

They are loud-mouthed boasters. “Loud-mouthed” (hyperonka) is swelling, bombastic, as in 2 Peter 2:18. Big words, little substance.

Admiring faces. “Showing favouritism” (thaumazontes prosōpa) is literally admiring faces: flattering the influential for profit (James 2:1–9). They said what their audience wanted to hear and were rewarded for it. Grumbling about God, they fawn over people who can pay.

Where Christians differ: does quoting 1 Enoch make it Scripture? The Ethiopian Orthodox Church includes 1 Enoch in its canon. This commentary’s view: Jude quotes one prophecy from 1 Enoch and affirms it as true, as Paul quoted true statements from pagan poets. This does not make the whole book inspired. Jesus and the apostles never treat 1 Enoch as Scripture, the Jewish people did not include it in the Hebrew Scriptures, and the church at large, though a few early writers valued it, did not receive it; it also contains much that is legendary. The canon is closed and does not include it.

Is 1 Enoch Scripture, then? Jude quotes a prophecy found in the book of 1 Enoch and says that Enoch truly prophesied this. Some think Jude regarded the book as inspired. The more likely reading is that Jude affirms this particular prophecy as true, as Paul quotes true lines from pagan poets (Acts 17:28; Titus 1:12), without endorsing the whole book, which neither the Jews nor the church at large received as Scripture. A true statement is true regardless of where it is found, and the Holy Spirit led Jude to use this one.

Is grumbling really that serious? Scripture treats it as far more serious than we do. Israel’s grumbling in the wilderness was counted as unbelief and rebellion against God (Numbers 14:27; 1 Corinthians 10:10). Grumbling says that God has given me less than I deserve and that he is not managing my life well. It poisons fellowship, spreads quickly, and is often the first sign of a heart drifting from God. The remedy is not pretending everything is fine, since the psalms are full of honest lament brought to God, but thankfulness and contentment (Philippians 2:14; 4:11–13). Lament takes the pain to God; grumbling talks about God behind his back.

How do I tell flattery from genuine encouragement? Encouragement tells the truth in love for the other person’s good; flattery tells pleasing untruths for the flatterer’s good. Encouragement is specific and honest and will also, when needed, include correction (Proverbs 27:6). Flattery is vague and excessive, is aimed especially at those with power or money, and never risks a hard word. If someone only ever tells you what you want to hear, be careful. And when you encourage others, give thanks for real evidences of grace in them, and be just as ready to say a difficult word gently. Giving flattery and enjoying it feed the same hunger: to be thought well of. A heart that already rests in God’s favour in Christ does not need to buy favour with flattery, and is much harder to buy with it.

In everyday life. Watch for grumbling in your own heart this week. Each time you catch yourself complaining, about the weather, the boss, the church, stop and name one specific gift of God instead, and ask the Spirit to teach you the contentment Paul learned in Christ (Philippians 4:11–13).
verseByVerse.note: Jude quotes 1 Enoch, a Jewish writing well known at the time. Quoting it does not make it Scripture; Paul also quoted pagan poets.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 17–23 — Hold Fast: The Call to the Faithful
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jude turns from the false teachers to the people he loves. The apostles foretold such scoffers, so their arrival is no reason to panic. Their task begins with their own life in God before it reaches out to rescue others.
verseByVerse.theology:
But You, Beloved

Build yourselves up in the faith, pray in the Holy Spirit, keep yourselves in God’s love, and wait for Christ’s mercy. Then show mercy to the wavering and snatch others from the fire.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The apostles had foretold scoffers in the last time.

Now: Meet each person where they are: patience for the doubting, urgency for the endangered, and care for yourself in the rescue.

verseByVerse.quote: But you must remember, beloved, the predictions of the apostles of our Lord Jesus Christ. They said to you, 'In the last time there will be scoffers, following their own ungodly passions.' It is these who cause divisions, worldly people, devoid of the Spirit.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Remember the predictions. Here the letter turns: Jude leaves the false teachers and speaks directly to the people he loves. “Predictions” (rhēmatōn) are words spoken beforehand. Paul warned that fierce wolves would come in (Acts 20:29–30) and that some would depart from the faith (1 Timothy 4:1); Peter warned of scoffers (2 Peter 3:3). Whoever knows that false teaching was foretold is less likely to be shaken when it arrives: the danger was on the map.

I have told you beforehand. Behind the apostles stands their Lord, who warned that false christs and false prophets would arise, and then said, “See, I have told you beforehand” (Matthew 24:24–25). So scoffers are no sign that Christ has lost control of his church; they fulfil his word. And the Lord who saw the danger coming has also said that the gates of hell will not prevail against his church (Matthew 16:18).

Scoffers. “Last time” is the whole period since Christ’s coming. “Scoffers” (empaiktai) are mockers, as in 2 Peter 3:3. Their teaching serves their way of life: they decide first how they want to live, and then shape their doctrine to excuse it.

Cause divisions. “Cause divisions” (apodiorizontes) is make separations. Perhaps they claimed to be a spiritual elite, with the dreams and the higher knowledge, above ordinary believers.

Worldly people. “Worldly” (psychikoi) is natural, unspiritual, as in 1 Corinthians 2:14 and James 3:15: living by mere human nature, as people who have never been born again, and not by the Spirit. They had religion, but everything about them could be explained without God.

Devoid of the Spirit. “Devoid of the Spirit” (pneuma mē echontes) is literally not having the Spirit. This is the decisive mark: they are not Christians at all (Romans 8:9), and Jude says it last. The one thing they most loudly claim is the one thing they most conspicuously lack. Where the Spirit’s fruit is love, joy and peace (Galatians 5:22–23), theirs is division, loose living, grumbling and self-promotion.

How do I know whether I have the Spirit? Every true believer has the Spirit; there is no second class of Christians who lack him (Romans 8:9; 1 Corinthians 12:13). The evidence is not dramatic experiences but the Spirit’s ordinary work: you confess Jesus as Lord from the heart (1 Corinthians 12:3); you cry to God as Father (Romans 8:15–16); you love Christ and his word; you fight sin and want holiness; you love other believers; and his fruit is growing in you, however slowly. If you see these, however faintly, the Spirit is at work. If you do not, ask God for his Spirit, for he gives the Spirit to those who ask him (Luke 11:13).

Is every division in the church caused by people like this? No. Some separations are necessary, when the gospel itself is denied (Galatians 1:8–9; 2 John 10). And many divisions among true believers come from ordinary sin, misunderstanding or honest disagreement on secondary matters, as between Paul and Barnabas (Acts 15:39). What marks Jude’s divisive people is that they split the church around themselves, claiming higher spirituality, while living for their own sinful desires. Before you separate from other believers, ask whether the issue is the gospel or your preference, and whether you have truly sought peace.

verseByVerse.quote: But you, beloved, building yourselves up in your most holy faith and praying in the Holy Spirit, keep yourselves in the love of God, waiting for the mercy of our Lord Jesus Christ that leads to eternal life. And have mercy on those who doubt; save others by snatching them out of the fire; to others show mercy with fear, hating even the garment stained by the flesh.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But you, beloved. Verses 20–21 have one command, “keep yourselves in the love of God”, and three activities around it: building, praying and waiting. The keeping is the command; the three activities are how it is done.

Building yourselves up. “Building up” (epoikodomountes) is active construction on the foundation of the apostolic faith, “most holy” because it comes from God (v. 3). Build your life on it, growing in Scripture and sound doctrine (Colossians 2:7; Acts 20:32). And the word is plural: this is done together, as a church.

Praying in the Holy Spirit. This is prayer guided and empowered by the Spirit, according to God’s will (Romans 8:26–27; Ephesians 6:18), so that our prayer comes into line with the Spirit’s own praying for us. The Spirit whom the scoffers lack (v. 19) helps believers pray.

Where Christians differ: does “praying in the Holy Spirit” mean praying in tongues? Some charismatic believers take it as speaking in tongues. Many who pray in this way are earnest believers who love Christ; the question here is only what Jude meant. This commentary’s view: Nothing in the context mentions tongues. Praying in the Spirit means praying under the Spirit’s guidance and in dependence on him, according to God’s will revealed in his word (Ephesians 6:18). All believers can and should pray this way.

Does praying in the Holy Spirit mean praying in tongues? Some Pentecostal and charismatic Christians read it so. But Paul uses similar words of all prayer, praying at all times in the Spirit (Ephesians 6:18), and nothing here mentions tongues. The more likely reading is prayer led and helped by the Spirit and in line with his will.

Keep yourselves in the love of God. The main command. “Keep” (tērēsate) is guard, preserve, echoing verse 1 (kept for Jesus Christ) and verse 6 (the angels who did not keep their position). Jude does not say, “Make God love you”; that is settled (v. 1). He says, stay where that love is known and enjoyed (John 15:9–10), as a man stays by the fire on a cold night. And we stay there imperfectly. The Son kept his Father’s commandments and abides in his love without fault, and he did it for us. We stand before God on his obedience, not ours.

If God keeps us, why are we told to keep ourselves in the love of God? Both are true (vv. 1, 24). God keeps his people, and he does it through their keeping themselves: building up their faith, praying and waiting for Christ’s mercy. Our effort is the means of his keeping, not a rival to it (Philippians 2:12–13). That is why Jude can end with full confidence in him who is able to keep you from stumbling.

Waiting for the mercy. “Waiting” (prosdechomenoi) is eagerly expecting. “Mercy” is the mercy Christ will show at his return, the mercy of verse 2 awaited in its fullest form. Even at the judgment, believers look for mercy, not for wages they have earned. Note the Trinity: Spirit, Father and Lord Jesus Christ, all in two verses.

Those who doubt. Verses 22–23 are a rescue mission, with three groups who need different help. “Those who doubt” (diakrinomenous) are believers unsettled by the false teachers. They need patient compassion, not condemnation.

Snatching them out of the fire. “Snatching” (harpazontes) is seizing quickly. Those on the edge of destruction need urgent rescue, as from a burning building; it recalls the brand (a burning stick) plucked from the burning (Amos 4:11).

Mercy with fear. The most deeply corrupted still receive mercy, but with caution, lest you be dragged down too (Galatians 6:1). “Garment stained” (spilōmenon chitōna) is a soiled undergarment, a picture of a life made dirty by sin (compare Zechariah 3:3–4); “the flesh” is our sinful nature. Show the person mercy, but keep clear of the sin.

A brand plucked from the fire. Jude’s pictures of rescue echo Zechariah 3. Joshua the high priest stands in filthy garments, with Satan accusing him. The LORD rebukes Satan and asks, “Is not this a brand plucked from the fire?” The filthy garments are taken away, and God promises to remove iniquity in a single day (Zechariah 3:1–9). That day came at the cross, where Christ was made sin for us (2 Corinthians 5:21). Every believer is a brand snatched from the fire, and that is why we go to others with mercy.

Textual note. The manuscripts differ in verses 22–23, some describing two groups, others three. The ESV follows the three-group reading, which has good early support; the King James Version, following later manuscripts, has two groups (“of some have compassion, making a difference: and others save with fear”).

A friend is doubting. What do I actually do? Start with mercy, as Jude says. Listen properly before you answer; find out what the doubt really is, whether intellectual, moral or born of suffering. Do not be shocked or impatient. Share your own struggles where it helps. Point to Christ himself more than to arguments: read a Gospel together, or a psalm of lament. Offer a good book if the question is intellectual, but stay with them; doubt is often lonely. Pray for them and with them. Keep them in the fellowship of the church. And be patient: many doubters come through to a stronger faith.

How do I help someone caught in sin without being pulled in myself? Go humbly, aware that you could fall too (Galatians 6:1). Do not go alone when the sin is one that tempts you; take a mature believer. Set clear boundaries: do not linger in the places or conversations where the sin lives. Keep your own walk with God close through prayer, Scripture and accountability. Speak clearly about the sin and warmly about Christ. If the person is unrepentant and the sin serious, involve the church’s elders (Matthew 18:15–17). Mercy is the goal; fear is the guard.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The letter that began with alarm ends in adoration. After so many examples of those who stumbled, Jude lifts our eyes to the God who is able to keep his people from stumbling and present them blameless with great joy. The doxology is the ground on which the whole letter stands.
verseByVerse.theology:
Him Who Is Able

Perseverance rests on God’s ability, not ours.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: A church under pressure was pointed to God’s glory, majesty, dominion and authority.

Now: The same God holds his people through every crisis, and will bring them home.

verseByVerse.quote: Now to him who is able to keep you from stumbling and to present you blameless before the presence of his glory with great joy, to the only God, our Savior, through Jesus Christ our Lord, be glory, majesty, dominion, and authority, before all time and now and forever. Amen.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Him who is able. “Able” (dynamenō) is has the power: God is not merely willing to keep his people; he is able. In a letter full of people who fell, this changes everything. Whatever you fear, the stumbling, the ground you might lose, the false teaching that might overwhelm you, the One who keeps you is stronger: he spoke creation into being and holds it together by the word of his power. “From stumbling” (aptaistous) is sure-footed, like a horse that does not stumble; the word appears nowhere else in the New Testament. He is not a safety net at the bottom of the cliff; he is a shepherd on the path, keeping the feet of his sheep.

Blameless with great joy. “Present” (stēsai) is cause to stand, the language of formal presentation before a king. “Blameless” (amōmous) is without blemish, the word used of a sacrifice without defect (Ephesians 5:27; Colossians 1:22). “Great joy” (agalliasis) is exultation, God’s joy and ours: the joy of the father running to meet his returning son (Luke 15:20). The homecoming of the saints is a joy to God.

Blameless because he was spotless. Blameless is the language of sacrifice, and it is used of one sacrifice above all: Christ offered himself without blemish to God (Hebrews 9:14; 1 Peter 1:19). That is how stumbling sinners can stand faultless in the presence of glory: the spotlessness they will wear is first his. And the joy of the presentation is his too, for it was for the joy set before him that he endured the cross (Hebrews 12:2).

Will I really be blameless? I know how much I still sin. Yes, and not because you will one day manage it yourself. Christ gave himself up for his church to present her to himself without spot or wrinkle (Ephesians 5:25–27). His blood has already cleansed you of guilt, and at his coming he will complete your sanctification: you will be like him, for you will see him as he is (1 John 3:2). Sanctification is the Spirit’s work of making you actually holy, begun at your new birth, growing now, and finished then; justification, by contrast, declared you righteous before God once and for all. There is no purgatory to pass through; the finished work of Christ is enough. Your present sin should make you humble and watchful, but not hopeless. The One who began a good work in you is the One who will bring it to completion (Philippians 1:6).

The only God, our Savior. “Our Saviour” is used of the Father here, as in 1 Timothy 1:1; more often the title belongs to Jesus. The salvation Christ accomplished is the Father’s salvation, and all glory is given to God through Christ. With the Spirit named in the praying (v. 20), Father, Son and Spirit are all here.

Glory, majesty, dominion, and authority. “Glory” (doxa) is the weight and radiance of God’s being; “majesty” (megalōsynē) his sovereign greatness; “dominion” (kratos) his power over all created things; “authority” (exousia) the right to rule. The false teachers rejected authority (v. 8); here all authority is ascribed to God.

Before all time. Before creation he was glorious; now, with false teachers in the church, he is glorious; and when every believer who feared stumbling is presented blameless, he will be glorious for ever. The letter that began with an alarm ends with the God who was never alarmed.

What if I am afraid that I will fall away? The fear itself, if it drives you to Christ, is a mercy. But your security does not rest on the strength of your grip; it rests on his. Jude does not say “to him who hopes you will manage”, but “to him who is able”. Christ prays for you (Hebrews 7:25), the Father holds you (John 10:29), and the Spirit seals you (Ephesians 1:13–14). So use the means Jude gave (vv. 20–21), and then rest. A child carried across a river is not safe because of how tightly he holds on, but because of the arms that hold him.

In everyday life. Learn this doxology by heart, and say it when you feel weakest: when you have fallen, when you fear you will, when the news about the church is bad. Let the last word in your mind be his ability, not your inability, and pray it over a struggling believer by name.

For worship. He is able. That is the last word of the letter, and it is enough to carry a stumbling church to glory. He will bring his people through every danger and every fall, and make them stand before his throne without blemish, with exultation, his and theirs together.

1.text: <sup>1</sup>Jude, a servant of Jesus Christ and brother of James, To those who are called, beloved in God the Father and kept for Jesus Christ:<sup>2</sup>May mercy, peace, and love be multiplied to you.<sup>3</sup>Beloved, although I was very eager to write to you about our common salvation, I found it necessary to write appealing to you to contend for the faith that was once for all delivered to the saints.<sup>4</sup>For certain people have crept in unnoticed who long ago were designated for this condemnation, ungodly people, who pervert the grace of our God into sensuality and deny our only Master and Lord, Jesus Christ.<sup>5</sup>Now I want to remind you, although you once fully knew it, that Jesus, who saved a people out of the land of Egypt, afterward destroyed those who did not believe.<sup>6</sup>And the angels who did not stay within their own position of authority, but left their proper dwelling, he has kept in eternal chains under gloomy darkness until the judgment of the great day—<sup>7</sup>just as Sodom and Gomorrah and the surrounding cities, which likewise indulged in sexual immorality and pursued unnatural desire, serve as an example by undergoing a punishment of eternal fire.<sup>8</sup>Yet in like manner these people also, relying on their dreams, defile the flesh, reject authority, and blaspheme the glorious ones.<sup>9</sup>But when the archangel Michael, contending with the devil, was disputing about the body of Moses, he did not presume to pronounce a blasphemous judgment, but said, “The Lord rebuke you.”<sup>10</sup>But these people blaspheme all that they do not understand, and they are destroyed by all that they, like unreasoning animals, understand instinctively.<sup>11</sup>Woe to them! For they walked in the way of Cain and abandoned themselves for the sake of gain to Balaam’s error and perished in Korah’s rebellion.<sup>12</sup>These are hidden reefs at your love feasts, as they feast with you without fear, shepherds feeding themselves; waterless clouds, swept along by winds; fruitless trees in late autumn, twice dead, uprooted;<sup>13</sup>wild waves of the sea, casting up the foam of their own shame; wandering stars, for whom the gloom of utter darkness has been reserved forever.<sup>14</sup>It was also about these that Enoch, the seventh from Adam, prophesied, saying, “Behold, the Lord comes with ten thousands of his holy ones,<sup>15</sup>to execute judgment on all and to convict all the ungodly of all their deeds of ungodliness that they have committed in such an ungodly way, and of all the harsh things that ungodly sinners have spoken against him.”<sup>16</sup>These are grumblers, malcontents, following their own sinful desires; they are loud-mouthed boasters, showing favoritism to gain advantage.<sup>17</sup>But you must remember, beloved, the predictions of the apostles of our Lord Jesus Christ.<sup>18</sup>They said to you, “In the last time there will be scoffers, following their own ungodly passions.”<sup>19</sup>It is these who cause divisions, worldly people, devoid of the Spirit.<sup>20</sup>But you, beloved, building yourselves up in your most holy faith and praying in the Holy Spirit,<sup>21</sup>keep yourselves in the love of God, waiting for the mercy of our Lord Jesus Christ that leads to eternal life.<sup>22</sup>And have mercy on those who doubt;<sup>23</sup>save others by snatching them out of the fire; to others show mercy with fear, hating even the garment stained by the flesh.<sup>24</sup>Now to him who is able to keep you from stumbling and to present you blameless before the presence of his glory with great joy,<sup>25</sup>to the only God, our Savior, through Jesus Christ our Lord, be glory, majesty, dominion, and authority, before all time and now and forever. Amen.
